gpucanvas

Put thousands of live DOM nodes on an infinite canvas: the GPU draws them, an editor selects,
moves and resizes them, shaders and transitions run on them, and an AI agent can read them and
point at them.

 

The same session on both sides: 5,000 live React screens, the same camera path, a message typed and sent. Left, every screen is plain DOM under a CSS transform. Right, gpucanvas. Recorded in Chrome on a MacBook Pro; the frame rates are measured live in each run. Run it yourself in the live demo.

- Canvas. Live React or plain DOM nodes, drawn by WebGPU in one instanced
 pass. Pan and zoom never touch the DOM, and clicks, typing and state still reach the real
 elements.
- Editor. Click to select, double-click to go a layer deeper, down to any element
 or React component. Move and resize with snapping guides.
- Shader effects. Run WGSL on live components: a glass lens, frost,
 shockwaves, glitch, VHS, or your own.
- Snapshots. Any node as an image, pixel diffs between versions, and a
 filmstrip of its history.
- Agent view. What is on the canvas as a short JSON tree with ids, and an
 image of any region, for an AI agent to read and point at.
- Transitions. Dissolve, wipe or fade a node out and another in, on the
 GPU, while both stay live.
- Marks. Arrows between elements, comment pins, notes and live cursors that
 follow the camera.

components. Recorded in Chrome from the demo.

How it works, with the benchmarks and what Chrome's HTML-in-Canvas does differently from the
explainer: gpucanvas: 5,000 Live React Screens on a WebGPU Infinite Canvas.

 Try it

Open berkantay.github.io/gpucanvas in Chrome 157 or
later. Thirty agent cursors build the first view, then the camera pulls out to all 5,000 screens.

- Click a screen to select it, double-click to go deeper, drag to move it. Double-click a text
 field to type in it, or switch the toolbar to Interact and use the screens like a normal page.
- In Interact, every button does something. Continue, Sign in and Back move the camera to the
 next screen like a clickable prototype, Notifications and More open panels, Export saves a
 CSV, Send adds the message and Share copies the link.
- The toolbar holds every setting: renderer, number of screens, Edit or Interact, what a click
 selects, the shader effect, the agent cursors and the theme. They apply live, and the URL
 remembers them.
- Pick a shader effect in the toolbar, or open one directly:
 glass,
 shockwave (click anywhere),
 frost,
 glitch.
- Select a screen and press D to dissolve it, W to wipe it, or S to save it as a PNG.
- In the console, agentView.describe() lists what is in view, and marks draws on it.
- Press b to run the benchmark tour, f to fit every screen in view, t to switch the theme.
- On a phone: pinch to zoom, drag to pan, tap to use a screen.

The GPU path needs WebGPU and HTML-in-Canvas. Chrome 157 and later on a computer has both on by
default, so the demo opens on the GPU path. On older Chrome or other Chromium builds, turn it on
with chrome://flags/ canvas-draw-element and relaunch.

Without HTML-in-Canvas the demo runs the DOM fallback with 1,000 screens and says so. Phones start
smaller so the tab is not killed for memory: 1,000 screens on the GPU path and 250 as DOM. Firefox,
Safari and every iPhone or iPad browser have no HTML-in-Canvas yet, so they run the DOM version and
say so.

Status: early (0.4). The API can still change.

 

 

Nodes stay real DOM: React state, events, CSS and accessibility work as usual. Where WebGPU and
HTML-in-Canvas are available (Chrome 157+), nodes are snapshotted into a GPU atlas and drawn in
one instanced draw call. Everywhere else it falls back to a CSS-transformed container with the
same API.

 Editing

 bindEditor turns the canvas into an editor: select, drill in, move and resize. The GPU draws
the outlines, 2 CSS pixels wide at any zoom, and they follow their element's layout. Names,
sizes, handles and snapping guides sit in a thin overlay above it.

 

A click selects the outermost layer under the pointer, a whole node. Each double-click goes one
layer deeper, and later clicks stay at that depth. Wrappers the size of their parent are skipped,
so every double-click visibly changes something.

 Input Does 
 ------------------ ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- 
 Double-click One layer deeper; on a text field, starts typing in it 
 Enter, Shift+Enter First child, parent 
 Tab, Shift+Tab Next and previous sibling 
 Escape Ends typing, cancels a drag, then goes up a layer, then clears 
 Drag Moves, snapping to the edges and centers of neighbors (Shift locks the axis) 
 Handles Resize (Shift on a corner keeps the ratio) 
 Drag on open space A box that selects the layers it touches, inside the layer you are in 

With the default trigger: 'shift-click' , the same works with Shift held, and clicks still reach
your components. A layer is an array of elements, so one layer can be a component that renders
several. pick decides the layers:

- 'node' : whole nodes only.
- 'element' : every element from the node down to the one under the pointer.
- a function of that element, returning the layers that hold it, outermost first.

In React, useEditor gives the selection as state, and pickComponents makes the layers React
components:

 

 pickComponents and componentOf read React's internal fibers, as click-to-component tools do.
Production builds usually minify component names, so mark components with your own attributes
when you need names there.

Colors are the selectionColor and hoverColor options. In the demo, the toolbar switches between
Edit and Interact (clicks reach the components) and picks components, elements or whole screens.
